meta.title: His Own
meta.skill_frame: Literary text: tell whose words a letter carries, and read which version did the work.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 6.0 over the three parts (103 words at FK 6.23, 113 words at FK 5.96, 105 words at FK 5.96). The load is two letters, one author who writes for other people, and a reason a formal letter failed.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for literary_text 4.2, Band 4.2, sequence 6. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A front office that writes letters for people who cannot, a leaking barn roof, and a farmer who says the words are not his.
source.avoided: No county, town, owner, or rent named. No claim about the law on repairs.

session.difficulty_basis: one complaint written twice by two hands, and the reason the shorter one worked

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: The man in the front office wrote letters for people who could not write them well, which in that county was more people than anyone admitted. He had a pen and a box of carbon paper and a way of turning a complaint into a paragraph. The tenant farmer came in about the roof of the barn on the lower place, which had leaked since March. The man asked his questions and wrote four hundred words about weather and neglect. He read the words back to the farmer and waited for him to say it was good. The farmer did not say that.
passage.part_2: The farmer said the letter did not sound like him, and the man said it was not meant to. He said the owner read letters of a certain kind, and that a letter from the front office was worth more than a letter from a barn. The farmer said the owner had never read a letter of any kind. Then he told the man about the two buckets under the beam and the stain down the north wall. He told him about the calf that stood in six inches of water in the corner box for a week in March. The man wrote it down as the farmer said it, without the weather.
passage.part_3: The second letter was shorter and had the buckets in it. The farmer read it standing up, with one finger under each line, and said that was the thing. The owner sent a man to look at the roof in nine days, which was faster than the front office had ever managed with four hundred words. The man put the carbon copy in the drawer with all the others. On the outside he wrote the farmer's name, and under the name he wrote two words: his own. The four hundred words went out of his head before the week was over, and the buckets stayed.

items.prompt: What does the man in the front office do?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. He writes letters for people who cannot write them well.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The first sentence says exactly that, and adds that there were more of them than anyone admitted.
tutor_only.tell: He writes letters for people who cannot write them well themselves.
help: The first sentence of the part says what his work is.
He has a pen, carbon paper, and a way of turning a complaint into a paragraph.
tutor_only.core_idea: He writes letters for people who cannot write them well.
accept_ideas: writes letters people cannot write themselves
not_required: what the office building looked like
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says he works on roofs
if_they_say.ask: The roof is what the farmer came about. What does the man do with a pen?

items.prompt: What was the first letter he wrote for the farmer about?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The leaking barn roof, in four hundred words about weather and neglect.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The part gives the roof leaking since March and the four hundred words he wrote.
tutor_only.tell: He wrote four hundred words about the leak, the weather, and neglect, and it was not the farmer's own account.
help: The sentence about the roof says how long it had leaked, and the next says what he wrote.
The letter was long, and it was about weather rather than about what the farmer saw.
tutor_only.core_idea: It was about the barn roof that had leaked since March, written as a complaint about weather and neglect.
accept_ideas: the roof on the lower place
four hundred words about the roof
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says it was about the calf in the water
if_they_say.ask: The calf belongs to the second letter. What is the first one about?

items.prompt: Why did the farmer say the first letter did not sound like him?

tutor_only.confirm: Yes. The words were the office's, written the way the office thought an owner would read.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The man answers that it was not meant to, and that the owner reads letters of a certain kind.
tutor_only.tell: The letter was written in the office's formal voice. The farmer would not have said any of it that way.
help: Read the farmer's objection and the man's answer straight after it.
The man's answer is about what kind of letter an owner reads.
accept_ideas: it was written the way the office writes
it was too formal to be him
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the letter had the wrong facts
if_they_say.ask: He does not correct a fact. What does he say about the sound of it?

tutor_only.full_idea: The letter carried the office's formal voice, and the farmer would not have put it that way.

items.prompt: What did the farmer give the man for the second letter?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The things he had seen: two buckets, a stain, and a calf standing in water.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The part lists the buckets, the stain, and the calf in six inches of water for a week.
tutor_only.tell: He gave the man what he had seen himself, the buckets, the stain, and the calf in the corner box.
help: The sentence after the man says the owner never reads letters lists the buckets and the stain.
The details are things a person standing in the barn would know.
accept_ideas: what he had seen in the barn
the calf standing in six inches of water
not_required: how many letters the man had in his drawer
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says he gave him a cheaper price
if_they_say.ask: No money is mentioned. What did the farmer describe in the barn?

tutor_only.full_idea: He gave the man the details he had lived with, the buckets, the stain, and the calf in the water.

items.prompt: The shorter letter got the owner out in nine days. What does the story show made the difference?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. The farmer's own details did, and the office's four hundred words did not.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The part sets nine days against four hundred words the office had never managed, and the drawer says his own.
tutor_only.tell: The second letter carried the farmer's own account of the barn. That is what moved the owner, and the label on the copy says whose it was.
help: Compare what the second letter had in it with what the first one had.
One letter has buckets in it. The other has weather and neglect.
tutor_only.core_idea: The farmer's own details made the letter work. His words, not the office's, moved the owner.
accept_ideas: the details he had seen made the difference
his own account did the work
not_required: how long the front office had waited before
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the shorter letter was cheaper to post
if_they_say.ask: Nothing turns on the post. What was in the shorter letter?

if_they_say.when: the student says the second letter used better words
if_they_say.ask: The man wrote fewer words and plainer ones. Whose account is inside them?
